answers.question: My club mate runs 70 miles a week before a marathon. I'm thinking of doubling to 80 next week to catch up, running twice a day. Would that work?
answers.answer:
No. Jumping from 40 to 80 mi in one week, with doubles, is the riskiest move you could make five weeks out.

- **The jump is too big.** You started this build at about 30 mi a week, and your biggest week so far was 53 mi. Even that left your legs heavy until Thursday.
- **The timing is wrong.** Extra mileage takes weeks to turn into fitness, but the tiredness and injury risk come straight away. Any gain would land around race week, when you need to be fresh.
- **Your club mate's 70 mi took years to build.** Their legs are used to it. Yours are used to 40 to 50 mi.
- **Running twice a day adds little here.** You run five days a week, so a second run mostly cuts into your recovery between the key sessions.

You are not behind. Your 6 mi at marathon pace on Wed Sep 16 averaged about 8:36/mi at effort 7/10, which is right where 3:45 needs you. Steady weeks will get you there: about 44 mi next week, a little more after that, then the taper.

new.analysis:
## How the week went
Sep 14 – 20 was the best week of this build because it matched the plan to the mile. You ran all five planned runs at their planned distances, 40 of 40 mi, and kept Monday and Friday as rest. Right now, that consistency is worth more than any single big session.

Your marathon-pace miles on Wednesday were even as well as on target. The splits in that stretch all sat within about 10 seconds of each other, with no fade at the end. Even pacing on fresh legs is what lets you hold the pace later on tired legs.

Your easy running is stable. Your easy runs held 139 bpm at about 9:50/mi for the third week in a row. The 15 mi long run stayed even from start to finish at effort 5/10.

## Why only 64 percent of your running was easy
The long run is the main reason the easy share was below 80 percent. It averaged 146 bpm, right on the line between zone 2 and zone 3, so over half of it counted as zone 3. Running the easy miles a few beats lower fixes this without costing you much pace.

Expect the share to be in the 60s again next week. Two harder sessions add warm-up, recovery and race-pace time that counts as harder running, and that is part of the plan.

## Why this plan
Next week goes up about 10 percent, to 44 mi. You have handled more than that before, and the long run stays the center of the week.

Threshold work on Wednesday and race pace on Sunday cover what the next five weeks need most. Threshold raises the pace you can hold comfortably. Race-pace miles late in a long run teach you to hold 8:35/mi when tired.

The two sessions are four days apart, so each gets full recovery. Treat Sunday as a practice race day. Use the shoes, gels and drinks you plan to race with, so nothing on Sun Nov 1 is new.

Do your two strength sessions on easy days, but not on Saturday. Monday and Friday stay full rest days.

## Where this is heading
Two or three more building weeks come before the taper starts in mid-October. Your longest remaining run will be about 18 to 20 mi, with race-pace miles in it. It will take about 3 hours. You have already run 20 mi once, so that distance will not be new.
